utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Daryl Mundis, and the case manager, Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Alexis Demirdjian, legal assistant for Mr. Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Fahrudin Ibrisimovic and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant, on behalf of Mr. Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber would like to greet everybody present, the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, as well as all the others present in the courtroom. Today we will continue hearing the witness that we heard yesterday. We are going to bring the witness into the courtroom, and after that we are going to tackle the issue of the forensic analysis of a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I hope that you are well rested because today we will continue your testimony that we started yesterday. I'm going to give the floor to the Defence, who indicated yesterday that they would need another half an hour for their cross-examination. Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Bourgon: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning, Mr. Hackshaw. When we left off yesterday, we were looking at a letter which we had received from the Prosecution, that you confirmed being familiar with. Do you remember this letter?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned yesterday that this letter -- you were aware of the fact that the letter basically said - and I quote from the letter - that "The perpetrators for such offences are generally unknown," and you acknowledged this information.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course, that this was something that made the task of the Prosecution difficult in trying to identify the fact whether there was any cases which had been referred to the military prosecutor for cases which are in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you left for your mission in June, you did not have, of course, any information which was provided to you by the Defence or any replies to this letter in giving you any names of perpetrators, did you?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't take any of that sort of material with me at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, urn not surprised, because if we had known who those Mujahedin were, maybe we would not be here today.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a possibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, a further complication in terms of your investigation or your mission, and you mentioned this yesterday, was that both in Zenica and Travnik there were a significant number of files missing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is absolutely correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to quote you from yesterday, you mentioned that "This was a serious flaw in the whole exercise."

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It complicated matters insofar as it meant that we had to -- if there were case files unavailable, we then had to use the registers in which they receipted or logged incoming correspondence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your mission in Central Bosnia lasted from the 2nd to the 5th of June, 2004; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the logs which we had, it appears to me that you arrived in Zenica on the 2nd, basically that you spent two days in Zenica and one day in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were accompanied, as you mentioned yesterday, with Mr. Michael Koehler. Now, he's a member of your team.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. He's an investigator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Macleod, Alasdair Macleod, is a member of the leadership team.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in response to my colleague yesterday, you mentioned that you were accompanied by an interpreter, but this was not mentioned in your statement, so I looked up in your notes and it appears that there were two interpreters.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes, there were two local interpreters with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were local, from the area?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: From -- well, they were based in the Sarajevo field office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, these interpreters, is there a reason why you did not mention this in your statement or should it have been mentioned in your statement? Because if you deal with documents, it's always important to know every person who is there.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, that's an oversight on my part. I just took it as common sense that the documentation would be certainly in a language that in this instance myself and Michael Koehler couldn't read and we would need to use the services of an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the third person on the team could read B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Alasdair Macleod can read B/C/S sufficiently to translate the material.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that allowed you to work - the three of you - simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the purpose of your visit, of course, was to go to both Zenica and Travnik and to visit the prosecution service.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that -- you were to examine the records held at both offices.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the objective was you'd review the records and you'd attempt to identify any records of crimes alleged in the indictment for which some kind of report would have been referred to the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can rephrase the question. Please do not hesitate to tell me if you do not understand my questions. Now, would I be right in taking it that your investigation assumption was as follows: If you find a file about an event alleged in the indictment which was referred to the military prosecutor, this would mean that the General Hadzihasanovic did take measures; and if you do not find such a file, it would mean that General Hadzihasanovic did not take measures to punish? Was that your investigation assumption?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: In very broad terms, I would say that's part of it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you spent a very short time, in terms of this mission, and you mentioned this yesterday, whereas you said that you were pressed for time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. It was a short period of time to cover a lot of ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also mentioned that for this reason when looking through all the files you focussed on the specific crimes rather than to look at everything, and that you were focussing on crimes against the person.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the initial stages. That's not correct. In the initial stages, the prosecution service in Zenica provided us with all the physical case files that they had or that we had asked for in relation to crimes where the perpetrators were known. They were the case files referred through the district military prosecutor and through the higher public prosecutor where the perpetrators were known. Those were the physical case files that were presented to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's just -- you were given, basically, according to your testimony during your examination-in-chief, you were basically given registers and a bunch of files; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you explained that amongst those files there were some that were neatly bound in particular or specific piles and others that were simply bundled loosely.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also explained yesterday - and I think that's important for the Trial Chamber to understand - that there were three types of registers. One was the KT register, which is the one where there is a known alleged perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this would mean that in this register the district military prosecutor receives some type of referral - and there are many types - and if there is someone who is the alleged perpetrator it goes in the KT register.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there's also a KTN register, and that is when the district military prosecutor receives information where a crime is alleged but there is no suspect. There is no alleged perpetrator so it goes into the KTN register.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you have the KTA register - I'll just spell it for the transcript: kilo, tango, alpha - which deals with miscellaneous correspondence referred to the military prosecutor dealing with either past cases or future cases.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it appears to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now -- of course, you just mentioned this, and I think this is also very important, because you were actually given separate registers for the district military prosecutor and for the high public prosecutor for the period you were looking for; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the reason for this, of course, you are aware is because if the alleged perpetrator is in the military, it is a file that goes to the high public -- sorry, it goes to the district military prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Although, we did find circumstances in the KTN civilian or higher public prosecution files where there was a combination of civilian persons and military personnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah, did -- thank you. Thank you for this answer, because this was my next question. The registers -- they gave you the register of the high public prosecutor because he has jurisdiction whenever an alleged crime was committed by both military and civilians together. And, of course, you were aware of this before you deployed to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not -- not -- no, I wasn't specifically, but I accept that that's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, taking from your statement, you were given registers for both the district military prosecutor, and that is, you were given a KT register, a KTN registers, and a KTA register, so three registers for the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for the high public prosecutor, you were given a KT register, a KTN register, but there was no KTA register.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you understand, and it was probably explained to you, that if a file comes at the office of the district military prosecutor, for example, with no alleged perpetrators, it would move into the KTN register.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that wasn't explained to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, but I mean -- sorry, we said that already, so I'm just trying to confirm now. I don't want to confuse you. The file arrives, and there's no alleged perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it goes in the register where you have no alleged perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the logical sequence of events, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, later on, if through some investigation a perpetrator is identified, it would then move into the KT register. It would move. The incoming information, they would take it away from the KTN register and then put it in the KT register.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. To be perfectly honest, I don't recall seeing any examples of movement beyond files being moved out of the -- away from the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about files. I'm just talking about the entry in the register.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that explained to you in any way or ...?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your statement, you say that because there was -- you confirmed that there was no KTA register for the high public prosecutor. KTA.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't one that I saw, but I just presumed that it was because the correspondence wasn't in abundance of that nature. Perhaps they shared a register.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in your statement you also say that the KTA register that was there was only for the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's probably correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can quote from your statement, unless you recall.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- no, I'm pretty sure that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also say in your statement that because there were so many files, that you decided to make a brief record of all the KT files; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: We decided to make a record of the KT files -- case files that were physically present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, again I quote, you could see for yourself that "There were multiple requests for investigation which had been submitted to the district military prosecutor for a wide variety of offences allegedly committed by military personnel."

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I further quote, in terms of your statement. When you did the same exercise with the high public prosecutor files, you said that due to time constraints you did not record the details for the vast majority of these files.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again I quote from your statement, just to be sure that -- you said that during all this exercise you focussed on serious crimes against the person and more particularly on murder and manslaughter.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there were two reasons probably for this, and I suggest this to you: One was the volume of file referred to the district military Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. prosecutor. Would that be one of the reasons?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the second reason could be the limited time at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's another reason. And there's also -- also part of the rationale for that exercise was that in the registers, victims' details where known were recorded, and I knew that the victims are also named in our indictment in respect of the murder counts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, when you -- so that's a third reason why you focussed on the crimes against the person, because you had names for victims sometimes in the register -- of the KT register.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, of course for this reason, if in the indictment there is no alleged perpetrator and there is no alleged victims, then you could not perform this exercise; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- that's correct. If I don't have the names of victims, it becomes very difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you -- if I look at the crimes against property, you did not look at the alleged crimes against property, because of course there are no alleged victims in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Zenica office we did, because there were case files present and all physical case files were checked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in Travnik you did not.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in Travnik we did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so maybe there are some files in Travnik which refer to crimes against property, but you can't tell for sure.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say undoubtedly there are. There were multiple files -- sorry, entries in the register of that nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I would say, to be more specific, that there could very well be files for crimes against property alleged in the indictment which would be in the Travnik files.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that's certainly probable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I -- if we recap based on this information: Now, we know that in the indictment Counts 5, 6, and 7 deal only with crimes against property.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to give you an example of one incident that you could find maybe in Travnik, and that was evidence that is here in this trial. And I refer you to -- I will now distribute some documents which I would like to show to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I've prepared these documents. Although it seems that we have a lot of documents, there are just a few of them that we will address in detail, and we will go through them very quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Mr. Hackshaw, I refer you to documents 2 and 3, about the -- where it says on the top "The Travnik church."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And for the record, I say that these are exhibits DH66 and DH67, which are both dated 8 June 1993. One is a criminal complaint, and one is a record on investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I take it that when you deployed to Travnik, because this is new evidence which was introduced in the trial, that you probably took these documents with you in order to verify the source of these documents in the Travnik prosecutor's office. Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you made aware that these two documents were entered in evidence in this trial?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of these documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I just ask this because I will ask some questions, but I will move on. Now, just to come back quickly on the issue of missing files. Can you confirm first that there were no KTN files present whatsoever in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were none presented to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I suggest to you that this was not a surprise, because if the perpetrator is unknown, then the case would still be open.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that makes perfect sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this, of course, brings about a further difficulty, because you were mentioned by the prosecutor that many of the files which remained open were transferred to the prosecution service within each municipality. Do you recall this information?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That was what was explained to me. Yeah, that was what was explained to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like to confirm, because when we talk about these files being transferred to the municipalities, to the prosecution service of the municipalities, my understanding is that you are aware that before going on your mission and you understood this, that the legal system at the time was divided into a two-tier system. Whereas if an offence called for a punishment of more than ten years then the case would be referred to the high public prosecutor, and that if a case or alleged offence called for a sentence of less than ten years it would then be given to the municipal prosecutor's office. Did you understand that before you went on your mission?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. That's a new piece of information to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you made aware that these municipal courts, the courts dealing -- and I say with - I do not have the time to go through the exercise of showing to you - but if what I say is correct, were you made aware that these municipal courts existed during the war as well as the office of the municipal prosecutor, that these things existed during the war? Were you made aware of this?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not specifically. No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if again, if what I say is correct, would you agree with me that if an offence during the war is committed by a soldier, by a member of the military, then automatically, that's an easy case, it goes to the district military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, with all due respect, I think my friend keeps addressing the wrong witness with his questions. This is an investigator. This is not a legal person. This is not a lawyer. These questions that are being asked, including the two that went above that I refrained from objecting to, are questions that are better suited to somebody with a legal mind. This witness cannot be expected to answer questions that arise from a legal basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this question was put yesterday. It's true that if you ask a question of a legal nature, this might be beyond the witness's understanding, unless the witness says that he has knowledge that would allow him to answer such questions. So take care when putting your questions so that you can see whether the witness can state his position with regard to certain legal matters. If that is the case, then do proceed; but otherwise, there's no point in wasting time, and Ms. Benjamin is quite right. This isn't the right witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to have certain clarifications from the main investigator on the basis of his understanding of the system. I wanted to know how he proceeded when -- before going to find the documents. I thought he'd have a minimum of knowledge about this matter. But I'll move on to another issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Could you please confirm, Mr. Hackshaw, that you were not aware of what I referred to earlier, the existence of the municipal courts and the municipal prosecutors during the war.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a recollection that the Travnik prosecutor mentioned that there were only military prosecutions conducted at Travnik and some -- and I recollect that he mentioned that there were also some basic municipal prosecutions conducted there as well. So based on that, I would say that yes, there probably were some municipal-level prosecutions conducted as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again, I'll move quickly, because -- to avoid -- my aim is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I'm not at all to put you on the spot and to get you to -- that's not my aim whatsoever. But if, for example, I would ask: Did you go to the Bugojno municipal court to try and obtain records for offences allegedly committed in Bugojno and that are in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you explained that in Travnik you had done about the same exercise as in Zenica but that you had done this in reverse due to a lack of time, which means that you focussed on the register because there were lots of files missing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the prosecutor also told you that there was a further problem, which was the disorganised state of the archives when the cantonal courts were merged with the municipal courts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, there were no KTA files or register present.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a KTA register present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this KTA was -- it was mentioned to you by the prosecutor that this was only a district military prosecutor KTA register and not a high public prosecutor register.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, and you can also confirm that there were no -- I mean, zero -- KTN files present. Now, the KTN is the file where is the alleged perpetrator is unknown. There was no files altogether. And I can refer you to your statement, because I don't want you to try and -- I'll just read from your statement, where you say "No actual cases, files prefixed with 'KTN' were physically present." Now, that's on page 3 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Your Honours, the delay is I'm just trying to allow the stenographer time to keep up with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate this, Mr. Hackshaw, because sometimes I forget, and the interpreters know this. I do my best, and sometimes I do forget. If we look at the fact that in the register you said that you really focussed on murder and manslaughter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I look for, for example, files of mistreatment, which would call -- you did not focus your attention on files of mistreatment, did you?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is, again, where difficulty arises in this situation. We certainly tried to focus on any serious assaults. Obviously our exercise is totally dependent on the manner in which a particular file is categorised when it is sent or received by the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you, Mr. Hackshaw, to simply turn to, in the information that you have in front of you, documents 4 and 5. Now, these were registers that we received from the Prosecution which come from the Zenica cantonal court. Document 4 is a register that deals with investigations, and number 5 is a register that deals with trial action or proceedings. Now, these are -- I do not want to mislead the Trial Chamber -- these, of course, are court records. But I'm just asking you: Is that the type of records that you were given? When you say "the registers," did they look like this?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were similar to this, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the type of information that you were provided with in -- to make your mission.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of the register, yes, the information was in a similar layout to this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move on to -- when we talk about -- because you did say that you focussed on murders or manslaughter, or at least where people died. For Dusina, you knew before going on your mission that we have a case referred to the district military prosecutor for Dusina. So I -- my understanding is that you took this with you on your mission.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My understanding is that no, we -- first of all, we didn't take any information, any documentation with us. Secondly, my understanding is that although I've seen limited documentation which I could -- which I believe related to the deaths of people in Dusina, I looked specifically around the time of events that Dusina occurred, namely the 26th of January, 1993 onwards, and I couldn't find any references to this particular crime. And that, to be perfectly honest, surprised me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you look at document number 6 in your package. Now, this, Mr. Hackshaw, is Prosecution Exhibit 332, and this is a document referred to the district military court in Zenica, and it's an official note which deals exactly with the case in Dusina. Did you find this document in your research in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just for -- in Dusina, did you -- when you were looking for information, although you focussed on the period of 1993 and early 1994, did you obtain any information as to the status of the Dusina investigation, if any?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I mention to you - and this was mentioned previously in this trial - of course, you know that in the indictment you have names of victims for Dusina. You would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you would also agree that you also have the name of one alleged perpetrator, namely Serif Patkovic.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're also aware that Mr. Patkovic is someone who was a witness in a previous trial before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know that on this occasion this witness denied being the author of this murder. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, this witness is an investigator. This witness is not involved in trials. This witness cannot be expected to answer those questions. This is an investigator. This is not a Defence counsel who was on the trial before or even the Prosecution, and it is unfair. My friend continues to do it over and over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But this investigator, who is a high-level investigator, he reads the press like everyone else and was familiar with the activities of the Tribunal, and he may have been familiar with a previous case in which Serif Patkovic apparently testified. So Defence counsel can ask the witness whether he was familiar with someone's testimony. He said yes, and then on the basis of that other questions can be put to the witness. If he's aware of it, he's aware of it; if not, he isn't. So please carry on, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This question is based on the fact that it concerns someone who according to the indictment was the perpetrator of a murder, and the witness is an investigator who was involved in investigating the murder, so I just want to know what sort of investigations he carried out with regard to the alleged perpetrator of the murder. Mr. President, if he knows nothing about, this he can tell me that. I suggest that this person, Serif Patkovic, testified in a case and the witness said that was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Mr. Hackshaw, you are aware of the contents of the testimony of Mr. Patkovic in this other case?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that he testified. I'm not aware of the specific detail. I am certainly aware that he denied involvement in the murder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, and are you aware that today in Zenica there is a trial going on with respect to the Dusina events?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that as part of this trial Mr. Patkovic is a witness and the accused is named Hakanovic and that he is the only person who is being charged with the Dusina events?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that a person by the name of Hakanovic is being tried for crimes that were committed in Dusina during 1993. I personally wasn't aware that Mr. Patkovic was a witness in that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move on to Susanj. And I'd like to refer you to a further document which is before you in your package, and that's documents 7 and 8. Now, Susanj is mentioned in the indictment, albeit not for crimes related to murders but at least to property. Is this document - Defence Exhibit 259, for the record - is this an exhibit that you are familiar with or that you have located in the district military prosecutor's files in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall personally having seen this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please put your question to the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] I'd like to refer you to document number 9, to take a look at the summary translation. Actually, it's not a summary translation. It's the full translation of the first part of this document. I would simply ask if you recall seeing this document, which deals with the killing of four people and the abduction of an HVO commander called Totic which was referred to the district military court. Do you recall seeing these documents as part of your mission?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall seeing this material, this part of my mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hackshaw, considering that you are -- you said yesterday that you were aware of the issues in this case. Would you agree with me that the Totic incident, although not charged in the indictment, is an issue in this case?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree. And I think anything with Mr. Totic's name in it should have been of interest to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to move quickly to the document number 10, which is in your file before you. This is a document that we looked at yesterday. And it talks in there -- this is a report from the Military Police Battalion. We've looked at it yesterday. I have one quick question: It says in this report "377 criminal reports were filed by the 3rd Corps Military Police Battalion." Can you confirm that it is not possible for you to say today whether you have seen these 377 criminal reports or if you have made a cross-reference between these reports and the documents you found in the Zenica prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, this -- yes, I would -- first of all, I would agree with you. It wasn't possible and we didn't check every single case file that was referred through, because, as I've explained, some were missing. However, I would -- I would in fact say that there were probably more than 377 cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were way more.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that would be normal, because that's only the military police of the 3rd Corps. But --

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other units may also have referred complaints.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, that's my misinterpretation. Yes, I would say that you're totally correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to refer you quickly to document number 13. This is Prosecution Exhibit 284, which I mention for the record, and it is dated the 10th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, which -- which one are we looking at again? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're looking at the document number 13, and it is called "Legality in the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And it's called -- at the top you see "Exhibit P284/English."

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is a Prosecution exhibit. Are you familiar with this exhibit, Mr. Hackshaw, given that it is a Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not personally familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I will simply move on, given that you are not familiar with the document. But just one question: Are you aware that this document was given to the Prosecution expert in order to make his opinion on whether measures were taken or not?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that there was a vast quantity of material given to the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could not say if this document --

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- expert witness. No, I couldn't. I couldn't comment on individual ones, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would refer you to another quick document, which is document number 14. And what I have for you in this document, it's called Prosecution Exhibit 192/E for English, a document dated 21 August 1993. I only include one page or two pages of this document, namely the front page, last page and page 13 which I wanted to refer to. Is this a document that you are familiar with as the leader of investigation team number 9?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I apologise. I'm struggling to find the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, I will -- there's a big report in the middle, and it's called "Exhibit P192/E."

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, my friend quite correctly tell it is witness that "I pull out one page," and then he turns to the witness and he says, "Are you familiar with this report?" Now, is that fair to the witness? He's pulled out one page and then he refers to report. Now, how could the witness be expected to comment on a page that he has pulled out of a report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This difficulty could be dealt with if the registrar provided the entire document, P192. Mr. Registrar, could you find document P192. That would be the simplest thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think that the objection was a pit premature. It's easier for the witness not to recognise a document if he's only provided with one page. The witness could have said, "I can't recognise the report on the basis of this one page," but we can now go a little further once the witness is shown the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document that the chief of investigations should remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Mr. Hackshaw, I'd like to turn to page 13 of this document, and there's simply one paragraph I'd like you to look at and to tell me, not on the basis of this document itself, but whether this paragraph relates to an issue, an investigation issue in this case.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And page 13, the third paragraph, which begins with "Special purpose production ..." Do you have this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would simply quote for the record: "Special purpose production. The military prosecutor's office and the military court also have an impact on command and control. Special purpose production manufactures items without prior consultation with the highest command, which should give priority to certain products at a particular time, depending on the development of combat operations." And then the important comment, where it says: "The military prosecutor's office and the military court are in the first place inefficient and they are not adjusting themselves to the need to change certain legal regulations." End of paragraph. My question to you, Mr. Hackshaw, is whether you knew that General Hadzihasanovic on a number of occasions had queried his superior command about the issue of the inefficiency of the court system, because for him it was an important issue?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware -- no, I'm not aware of specific incidences where the general did that. However --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you quickly, Mr. Hackshaw, to another document, document 19 -- no, sorry. Sorry, I will issue this document which I have with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is a document which is already in evidence. This is DH158. This is the fifth document in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] I would ask you, Mr. Hackshaw, whether you are familiar with the existence of a military disciplinary court within the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document appears to be -- "In order for the military disciplinary court of the 3rd Corps Command to become operational." So yes. Clearly from this document it appears that they're trying to get the necessary appointments to get such an organ in place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this an issue that you are familiar with in your capacity as team leader for investigation team 9?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say only vaguely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then I will move on. Thank you very much, Mr. Hackshaw. I'll move on to the last part of my cross-examination, simply dealing that -- about -- would you agree with me that in terms for the military commander to take the necessary and reasonable measures to punish - now, I'm not referring to prevent, which is a different issue - you would agree with me?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the measures to punish, would you agree with me that there are other measures that a commander may take to punish the perpetrator of an alleged crime?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I hate to be a nuisance. This witness is not a military expert. This witness does not have any legal expertise. This is a mere investigator who is out investigating documents. He cannot be expected to give an opinion that involves the military and involves law. It is totally unfair to the witness. And I think my friend has to find the correct witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Again your question was too technical for the witness. And I would like to say that when you put questions to him he automatically turns to the right, and this shows that the question is ill-suited for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm going to rephrase the questions, and I will be more precise in order to -- not to embarrass the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] Would you confirm that -- we know that you've been involved in this investigation since 1999. Have you investigated other areas than issues forwarded to the district military prosecutor in order to find out whether measures had been taken or not?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't really understand. If you're asking me whether Mr. Hadzihasanovic had other means to deal with crimes, I would say he's in a much better position to answer that than myself, given that he was the commander and given his previous background with the military police. I would say -- I personally can only assume that a military commander is bound by the rules and regulations of either the law or military law. If there is specific flexibility within those laws to deal with serious criminal offending through other means than the court, then so be it, but I don't believe that I'm the right person to give a professional opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hackshaw. I'm simply asking you -- my question is very, very clear, in terms of -- you investigated in Zenica whether cases had been referred to the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do other investigation of other types linked to the issue of whether measures had been taken or not?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't personally, but I know others did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what would you have looked at?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- persons who, I suppose, could be considered experts or specialists in these roles were spoken to, and certainly the court records, I understand, at both the Zenica and Travnik court were also looked at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move quickly based on this answer, because I had a couple of questions related to. But if I ask you whether you looked at -- because you looked at court records -- did you look at whether there were any trials which took place before the special military court? Is this an issue that you investigated?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not that I did. I understand that we looked -- or members of the team looked at the records that were kept at the Zenica and Travnik courts; however, no detailed analysis was done of that, because my understanding is that it didn't encapsulate necessarily all that had or should have been referred through the district military prosecution service. For example, if a file was stayed or if a file was rejected, then it would never get through to the court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to make it -- to avoid any confusion, are you familiar with the body called special military court?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if you are familiar, you know that this court is one which can be convened only by a brigade commander and up, on the authorisation of a superior commander.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be guided by what you say on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because that's important. Because if you tell me you're familiar, I just want to know to what extent you're familiar, in terms of looking for whether this body ever worked.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not specific of the -- I'm not knowledgeable of the specifics of workings of these organs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone your team look in the records to find out any traces of trials or referrals to a special military court?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to research that question further. I can't give you a categorical yes or no. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I talk about the military disciplinary court of the 3rd Corps, is this a body that you are familiar with?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you or someone in investigation team number 9 looked for the records of the military disciplinary court to see which complaints had been handled by this court?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm not 100 per cent sure. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would I be correct in saying that any disciplinary action handled by a brigade commander, the records within each unit -- that no one ever looked at the disciplinary records within all the brigades? Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it would be fair. I don't know. I don't know whether anybody specifically looked at those records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you know that of course -- and again, this is a technical question. I think it's basic for your investigation, but if you don't know, please answer you don't know. Did you know that if a soldier committed an offence, as a citizen of Bosnia he was liable for -- or liable to the law as any other citizen? Did you understand this? If you did not understand this, please say so. I just thought that -- was this a factor in your investigation?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was certainly evident that soldiers were subject to the provisions of the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I think I will simply ask you two more questions and this will be it, and one is: The fact -- no, I will refrain from this question, because maybe you're not, I guess, qualified for the question, because it's more legal. One last question: With respect to the music school. Now, the music school is an issue that was an issue in this case; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that the music school is an issue whereby there is a trial going on right now in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hackshaw. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there are two documents that I would like to tender into evidence either immediately or later on at your convenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe later would be best. The other Defence team, do they have any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, we do have a few questions for this witness. Cross-examined by Mr. Ibrisimovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Hackshaw. Mr. Bourgon has asked you whether you're familiar with the case that is being tried in Zenica with regard to the music school and you said that you were not familiar with that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the prosecutor's office in Zenica, they didn't tell you anything about a trial being conducted in Zenica with regard to the developments in the music school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't mention that court case at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will probably be surprised if I tell you that already in November 1995 the public prosecutor's office in Vitez instigated an investigation regarding the developments in the music school during the year 1993. Is this going to come as a surprise to you if I mention that?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To be perfectly honest with you, it doesn't come as a surprise at all. I think the events that occurred in the Zenica Music School were certainly no public secret, even during the time that this detention facility was running. So no, it's no surprise to me at all that the local authorities eventually took some affirmative action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to avoid confusion, the public prosecutor's office in Vitez forwarded all these documents to the public prosecutor's office in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm going to be putting questions to the witness, and I'm going to show him a document that the Prosecutor deems to be confidential. I would kindly ask you to order to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we will move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Prosecution to see whether they have any re-examination, the Defence asked us to admit into evidence a document that the Defence has obtained. We would like to be clear on one thing: You have been put a question, but the question was complex. I would like to ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to go into private session, Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Benjamin, you may ask your question again in open session now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hackshaw, it refers to the investigations and to how the conduct of the investigations re the pre-trial stage, indictment stage. Could you please answer for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Investigations continue through all phases that you've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my learned friend alluded to the system of the courts, and I'm not sure -- and for the benefit of the Trial Chamber maybe you can explain to us -- was it -- did you find a flaw in the court system or was the flaw in the exercise of your duties, how you conducted the investigations?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: The specific relationship to the exercise that we carried out between the 2nd and the 5th of June, 2004 -- it's correct that I mentioned that there were flaws. Those flaws, I believe, occurred because of a number of reasons, but principally it was because we were reliant on the information that was available to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as team -- or as acting team leader, sorry -- you had in your command -- under your command how many subordinates?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have immediately available to me seven investigators, three criminal analysts, and four language assistants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible, then, that you would not physically see all documents that are recorded specifically for this trial? Is it possible?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is the end of the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll ask you a few general questions, and the Judge to my left will ask you more specific questions about what you did when you visited the courts. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In general terms, and I will be very rapid, before you were a policeman, did you serve in the army in New Zealand?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't serve prior to joining the police. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a policeman in New Zealand - you said that you worked as a policeman for 15 years - did you get involved in problems that had to do with the New Zealand army? Did you have any military competence?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very, very limited, Your Honour. Very limited. I mean, I can only specifically recall a number of incidents where military personnel were arrested for what I would consider low-level incidents. And beyond those, other than playing Rugby Union for an army rugby team, it's very limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have been told that you were the chief investigator of team 9. When the investigation started, what was the name of the chief in team number 9?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: The team leader at that point in time was -- his name was Nikolai Mikailov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So thanks to you we've been told that the Prosecution had a number of teams and they were numbered. How many teams are there in all?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: At moment -- there were 11; some of them have now been merged. There is now less than 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So among the teams, were there common working meetings? For example, yesterday it was said that there was the Blaskic case that had been dealt with by another team. But did all the teams meet to exchange ideas, discuss the methods you followed and the information you had? Were there such exchanges that involved all the teams?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: On a global level, it's my understanding that the senior trial attorneys meet on a regular basis, I think normally every morning. And I've never been party to those meetings; however, I understand that all sorts of issues are discussed that impact the entire OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were there working meetings between the Deputy Prosecutor, the investigators, and all the teams? Did these meetings have to do with specific themes, or was there communication that was exchanged between everyone; or was everyone involved in his own particular field and there were no links established between these people? What was your experience as an investigator?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within our own team, we used to hold regular weekly meetings where all the team were -- who were in the office were expected to participate. These were chaired by the senior trial attorney and in his absence, the deputy chief of investigations. At these meetings, all range of issues were discussed. Beyond that, where there were specific issues for specific investigation projects, there were regular meetings held when and if issues arose or matters needed to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What degree of autonomy did an investigator have with regard to the deputy? The chief investigator - and that's what you were - did the chief investigator have very precise instructions? Or did the investigator have a degree of autonomy, as far as how he conducted his investigation was concerned? Or did the investigator simply do what he was told to do?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The investigator or the senior trial attorney or one of the trial attorneys or one of the analysts would -- in common terms would identify issues that they believed we needed to focus on, and those were generally discussed in a group forum and where decisions were ultimately made generally by the senior trial attorney or pre-indictment by the trial attorney, where subsequent action was discussed and agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But you're not answering my question, which is very specific. But I will help you. You went to visit the local courts and to visit the archives. We'll go back to that. But, for example, if you discover in files that a case that's been registered with the military prosecutor was transferred to the civilian prosecutor, in such a case did you have the autonomy to go to see the civilian prosecutor to check this without having to phone the Prosecutor to receive instructions? As you can see, my question is very specific. In such a case, what would you do? Would you conduct your investigation quite independently, or would you come back here or phone in order to request instructions as to how you should proceed?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the majority of cases, you would -- if you were in the field and you discovered that there was a tangent that you felt merited further investigation, the common practice would be that you would report back to either the trial attorney or the senior trial attorney or whoever was available to take your call and you would obtain some form of direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But why draft a report if you yourself could go and check matters? One has the impression that you wouldn't do anything without contacting those above you, whereas an investigator should be able to do things without having his superior authorising him to do so. That's -- those are the basics. In the case that I mentioned, were you obliged to submit a report, to make a report?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You -- but where possible you were obliged to exercise common sense. And there are -- beyond the actual investigation issues, there are another number of issues that need to be considered before you go off doing something which is not part of the original plan. For example, if got the opportunity to have an impromptu meeting with somebody who may be of future reference to the case, then naturally you would go off and you would have that particular meeting. But if you were going off to interview -- if a new witness came to light, then common sense says that you, first of all, want to obtain as much information about that person as possible. So therefore, if time allows, you take the necessary precautionary measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have one last question. As you can well imagine, I have a lot of other questions I could put to you, but I'll let the other Judges ask you their questions. My last question is as follows: You conducted an investigation into how the 3rd Corps operated. This involved high-level officers, grass roots officers, et cetera. In a classical type -- in a traditional type of investigation, in New Zealand, for example, if there is a group that may be charged with violations of some kind, wouldn't the police procedure involve hearing all the members of that group and then, in the case of the 3rd Corps, wouldn't it have been necessary for a policeman to take written statements from all the members of the military within the 3rd Corps? I would like to hear what your opinion is about this subject; that is to say, about the chief, the deputy chief, the third in command, et cetera, right down to the rank and file. So why does it appear that this wasn't done in this investigation? If you can answer the question, say so; but if not, just say that you aren't capable of answering it.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I can answer it. I think we have to exercise caution. I think if we endeavoured to interview every personality involved, one, we would face serious problems with time constraints. I think also we have to assess individual culpability, and yeah, I think, really, each individual we speak to has to be assessed on their merits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in terms of an investigator's technique, initially the investigator shouldn't have any assumptions and within the framework of an investigation the investigator should interview a number of witnesses without these witnesses being accused or suspects. So this is a very general technique. One interviews a number of people and one obtains certain information, certain basic information that guides you. This is what you must have done in New Zealand. You weren't told to interview such and such a person if there was no information to start with. Why didn't you follow such a procedure rather than just target certain people, rather than just select certain people? Is there any explanation that you could provide us with?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really, other than to say that, as I think I mentioned before, certainly at home and the practice is similar here, you would try and make a fair assessment of anybody that you wanted to speak to prior to speaking to them. So in many respects, often it's difficult to go in without making an assumption, because information that you're provided with, particularly about criminality of people, is relevant to the task at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. One of the other Judges has some questions for you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hackshaw. I would like to discuss with you the way you proceeded with your investigation, how you did it, what problems you met, and what conclusions you could make or draw or not draw on the basis of what you then did. Now, we listened to you this morning and yesterday, and we also received - it is perhaps good for you to know - a written statement that was not signed, not dated, but of which you said yesterday, "This is something I have written in preparation of my hearing as a witness." Well, if you look at the written declaration and what you said yesterday and this morning, I would be inclined to conclude that most of the things you have written in your declaration you have also said and confirmed during the hearings of yesterday and tomorrow [sic], especially due to the questions put to you by the Defence. There are still some details that you have not brought forward during these meetings of today and yesterday, and I take the liberty to put to you questions on that too, and I hope that the parties will not object to that. The first question that I have to put to you concerns a matter that has already been raised this morning, and they relate to the nature of the files you have seen, the registers you have seen in Zenica and in Travnik. You said there were three registers: KT, KTN, KTA. The fact is that we also have been given by the Prosecution documents with the same letters, "KT," "KTN." And my question to you would be: Could you compare some pages of the documents we have gotten from the Prosecution to decide on the admissibility of these documents with what you have seen physically in Travnik and Zenica as being the registers of the Prosecution? I have some reasons -- several reasons to ask you this, and I will explain them to you, of course, but first I would like the registrar to show you a few pages from the contested exhibit 506, if you have them. Otherwise, I could provide it to you personally, if you want that. We received a few weeks ago - no, I must say some ten days ago, perhaps - six binders of material from the two military district courts -- district military courts; all in all, I think some 1.000 pages maybe. And my question to you is: Look at these pages carefully. They are in B/C/S. I have a translation -- a provisional translation of pages -- I show it to you in English if you need. But on the face of it, what you are seeing now, are you able to tell us whether these are the same registers as you have seen on the spot?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: They look similar, but there -- from memory, the actual registers we reviewed were prefixed with "KT," "KTN," or "KTA." Now, the first column should have -- should reflect those numbers, But I'm -- I couldn't be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I think one of the counsel for the Defence want to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we place this on the ELMO so that we can follow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: For clarification, I may say that these are pages that are rather similar to what you showed the -- but different pages, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These -- again, it certainly looks a similar format to that which was contained in the registers we looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But not quite the same, maybe.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me correctly, in the registers we looked at they would have the KT reference number - for example, number 1 - and then it would be a "/" and then the year that they related to. But I could be completely wrong there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, one of the reasons I'm asking you this is the following: You mentioned several times that you found names of victims, individual victims on the registers of the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Now, in the pages that I show you, there is no special place to note the names of the victims. There are 30 numbers on top, as you see, and each correspond to a certain type of data. There is no separate row or column on data with regard to victims, and that is one of the reasons why I ask you are these the same documents or are they different.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then they must be different. The front of it has the reference prefix "KI" and that I'm not familiar with. Although, I understand -- I think "KI" relates to a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Known accused or known suspect.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: "KT" were the files -- the registers that we reviewed that related to known perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: "KT" and "KTN." Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And this is KI.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, kilo India.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I can't confirm, but I think that relates to investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: It may be, yes. Have you seen on the spot in both places not only the registers you have told us about but also this kind of registers?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any of those personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And are you familiar with the way tribunals or courts in general in different jurisdictions do file cases? Have you been told about a system of filing cases in Zenica and Travnik?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not beyond what was explained to me at the offices of the prosecution service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, let me give you an example of why I'm -- of a situation which may explain why I'm asking the question. In some countries, for instance, the public prosecutor and the courts have registrarily -- separate registration systems, totally independent from each other. In other countries, certainly in the past they would use the same registration system. So there would be a general registration system both for the courts and judges on the one hand, and the prosecutor. And that is a type of -- that is a kind of method you may still find in many European countries, although these things are changing. So this is a question for me: What type of registration was used in Bosnia at the time? Did they have a common registration system or did they have separate registration systems? But I think you cannot -- not answer that question.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only tell you what I encountered at the offices of the prosecution service in both Zenica and Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that was the KT system, the KTN system, and the KTA system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
