utterances.text: Yeah. Now, as you may have gathered from these few pages that I have given you, this is quite an extensive or quite a broad manner of recording data. It begins with the date the case came in or the documents came in, the name, other data. Then you have quite a few positions for articles in the Criminal Code, and then you have still more positions for what happened with the case. Has an investigation been asked? Has there been an indictment? Has there been a conviction? Has there been an appeal? Et cetera. So it's a very broad range.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did you see the same range in the registers you consulted?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: The same details and same possibilities of registering all kinds of data?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So, so far about these registers. You may take -- give back the ... Now, to continue our discussion of your investigation. Did you with your team before you went to Zenica and Travnik, did you have a look at those documents I showed you?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. I think one of the other members on the team had been involved in collecting records from the Zenica and Travnik courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: But as I mentioned before, no detailed analysis of that was conducted, because it was, based on the information that we had received, it appeared to be a flawed exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But you didn't discuss in your team together what he had seen or what he had --

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't discuss it with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't say categorically that he didn't discuss it with members of the trial team, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: If you didn't have a look at these documents before you went to Bosnia, then I take it that you could not predict what kind of material you would need and how much time you would need to study that material.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's a very fair assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So in that sense, they must have been a surprise to you.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: A surprise in what nature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: There must have been a surprise that the material was far more voluminous than you thought when you went to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was always the potential for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Because you said that was three-days exercise. Those are your words of yesterday. Tomorrow again you said, "We have spent two days in Zenica and one in Travnik," all in all three.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And that may have been too short to realise what you intended to do.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Definitely. Okay. One other question of an introductory nature: The kind of investigations that you were doing at the time is a type of investigation that is often done by professional criminologists or social scientists for different purposes, of course, but the research consisting of a systematic analyst of police documents or public prosecutor's documents or court documents is often done in that field. And my question to you is: Was any of the three of you - because I understand you were three -

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: -- familiar with analysing techniques used in criminology or social science?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is -- I would say probably the most likely candidate - and I can't say categorically - would be Alasdair Macleod, who's part of the leadership research team. He's -- a lot of his work is more document-orientated and analysis-orientated. And he would have -- yeah, he would have probably had a greater understanding than myself or Michael Koehler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. It is -- basically it is a quantitative analysis, isn't it? And that is different from interviewing a witness or looking at the authenticity of a document or that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Although, in saying that, it's still simply -- I mean, in its most simple form, it's still reviewing material, written material and subsequently making an analysis of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Now, I come to the second topic to discuss with you, the missing material and the place where the missing material might be. I understand that from your testimony this morning and yesterday and also from your written statement that when you arrived in Zenica not all files were present. And if I say "all files," you would -- I would say all files that -- of which you would find the reference in a register.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You said all the KTN files -- none of the KTN files were there.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So there are two kinds of case files: There are the KT files and there are the KTN files. And in the third place you have the KTA with correspondence, but that doesn't contain its own files, I suppose; or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't get the opportunity to review any of the actual -- that correspondence beyond what was collated in the register. So I can't comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So there were KT files present and there were KTN files that were not present.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: As far as the KT files are concerned, did you have a complete collection or -- or were even in this category some files missing?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were clearly a number of files missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Could you express how many?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, I -- not accurately. I would have to physically count the number that we checked and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So it's somewhere in --

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But I would have to check --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You recorded it, anyhow.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: We recorded -- for the KT files that went through the military -- district military prosecutor, we recorded details of every case file that we reviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And would you be able to express this in a percentage? Say you have the KT registers and they make clear how many cases have been registered and you could compare the actual case files with the register and say, "Well, I've seen 80 per cent or 90 per cent or 40 per cent," or whatever.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be possible, Your Honour, but I would have to physically do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You can't recall at the moment?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Not even in the vaguest sense? It is important for me to know, so ...

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the vaguest sense, I would probably say 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: 50 per cent. So. And the KTN files were not present; that is 100 per cent, so to speak; right?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Could you tell us, if you recall, how many cases were registered in both categories, in both kind of registers?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- I think in -- I think I have a note in my notebook that in the KT military prosecution register --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for 1993, I think there was 780.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And can you recall what was the number for the KTN?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. I would have to refer to my notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Would it be more? Less?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: How much less would you say?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe -- if it's all right to be vague, I would probably say 50 per cent less.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: 50. Five-zero. Considerably less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. So almost half then.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So the number of KT files were more numerous than the number of the -- the KT cases were more numerous than the KTN cases.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But you haven't quite kept details on that.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in my head, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I don't know whether these documents I showed you a fragment of would enable us to make a count, but that has to be seen. Now, the KTN files, you said, were not available. Did you ask why they were not available?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I asked only why there appeared to be files missing, and the only explanation I was given at the Zenica office --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was that there were likely to be files missing because they had been forwarded at the closure of the district military prosecution files, files were forwarded out to the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes. So these were the files that you were already -- discussed tomorrow with Mr. Bourgon. As far as the KT files are concerned, that cannot be the explanation because they were known perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, because there were KT files, because -- that we established from the registers that had been farmed out to a municipal level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Oh, there were.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, there were. And it was only those in Zenica -- the only KT files that were missing that we checked or cross-checked in the register were those for serious crimes against the person. And there were, there were files that had been -- well, that according to their explanation was still open at the end of the war and subsequently forwarded to the municipal level. Now ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So just to be absolutely sure what you're saying, because it's very easy to make mistakes for me. The KT files were known perpetrators but not all cases were closed and those who had not been closed were referred to the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was exactly the explanation I received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. And what then happened with the KTN files?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You didn't -- they didn't tell you?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And you didn't ask them?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You have not the slightest idea where they might be.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I see. The same is true for Travnik or even more so, I have the impression. You said yesterday and this morning there were no case files in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Only registers.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were KT files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: There were KT files.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes. But was the collection of KT files complete, or were a number of again missing?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In many respects, although the prosecutor that we spoke to clearly indicated that the archives were in a disorganised state, those that took care of us had assisted us considerably in some preparation that they had done prior to us getting there. And one of the -- it's my understanding one of the things they had done was they had got an intern who was working there to go through the files and to identify those that were missing, and that allowed us to move through the operation much more quickly, and effectively work in reverse as a consequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understand you completely, but let me ask the following question: Due to the disorganised state of the documentation or the archives which you also mentioned in your report, could there have been a number of case files that were in the building, so to speak, without you being able to consult them?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is certainly a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: That is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. And you cannot make a quantitative estimate about it, I think.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. All I can say is that on occasion - and I think it was -- I think it was only once - there was a file that was supposed to be missing that we actually found amongst the actual case files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. And could you tell me, which will be difficult, I understand now, but could you give me an estimate of how many KT files you found in relation to how many entries in the KT registers? What percentage would you have seen in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very difficult, because what we did at Travnik was we -- as I mentioned, we worked in reverse. So we effectively --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and at Travnik we only focussed on the serious crimes against the persons. So what we did was we, first of all, was we compiled lists from the register of the offences or the codes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yeah, I understand.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then we identified those that were related to murder, manslaughter, involuntarily manslaughter and serious assaults. And we then went through the case files that related to those specific entries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes. The reverse method, you called it.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: An appropriate name, I would say.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And the KTN files there, were none of them available or present in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And again, my question is: Did you discuss with the authorities there where they might be or have gone?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: No? Why not, I must say?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think because we were so busy going through the physical material that was present that we just focussed on what was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, if you realised that in both places - Zenica and Travnik - the KTN files are missing and not the KT files, that might suggesting that there is some sort of reason for it, that they might be stored somewhere else or ...

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: It seems more than a coincidence, I might say, although you never know.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My opinion would be that because they are unknown perpetrator files, they may well be archived elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: That's your estimate.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my assumption, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Assumption, rather. Okay. Well, now, you have this morning especially said, "We made a selection. We limited ourselves to crimes against the person or to -- only to murder and manslaughter," for instance.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: This is something that I would like to put to you questions about, and I need to some extent your written text for that, because you used different formulas for describing what you did, and I would like to check whether all these formulas are of the same content. The first category I met in your report, and you said it also this morning, were crimes against a person, particularly murder and manslaughter. That particularly is, of course, fascinating, and crimes against a person is a very vague concept. So what do you mean if you say "crimes against a person, particularly murder and manslaughter"?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply, I suppose it's a colloquialism from my days in the New Zealand police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: We really roughly categorise crimes into two distinct areas, crimes against the person and crimes against property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crimes against the person - and it's a loose definition, obviously - but crimes against the person, I mean where you have -- the victims have been subjected to some form of violence or -- yeah, I mean, even aggravated robbery I would put into the category of a crime against the person, because it involves -- although it may not involve actual physical violence, it can certainly involve threats of actual physical violence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Threats would count as violence.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. Now, a second formula that I've found in your report is more extensive. It says "serious crimes against a person, including grevious bodily harm, robbery, and aggravated robbery or burglary." That corresponds with what you said a few seconds ago. Does this cover a larger field than your first formula, or is it intended to express the same thing?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's intended to express the same thing, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. So if you read "crimes against a person, particularly murder and manslaughter," you must be aware that this may also include aggravated burglary then.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Aggravated burglary, aggravated robbery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the third and last formulae is crime related to murder, manslaughter, involving grievous bodily harm, violent acts of behaviour, robber and aggravated robbery. That again is the same thing, I understand.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So the basic distinction is crimes against the person and crimes against property.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: This is the basis of your distinction.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the two loose categories I refer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And if one would meet a person in the street with valuable goods, one would say, "You get me the goods or otherwise I do something to you," would that be burglary?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would say -- I would categorise that as a robbery or an aggravated robbery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Because of the element of threat.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And if you take goods from a person who is not present, he's away, he's not in his house or whatever?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Then that would not be a crime against the person, then.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I would categorise that as a theft or a burglary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. And an aggravated burglary is something involving physical violence.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or aggravating features to the crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: The following question is: Your category, you suggested more or less that -- your distinction between these kinds of crimes came from your own background in New Zealand.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: That's right. And what I would like to know is whether you used this distinction also looking at the registers. In other words, were you looking at the articles mentioned in the registers to determine?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So you had a Criminal Code next to you and you -- or this was explained to you, this is a crime against a person, or this is a --

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the -- we had a republic Criminal Code, and the intern that assisted us throughout the day had that present at Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So she or he basically said this number, 193, is a crime against a person.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Or -- no, no, sorry. That's not correct. They would give us the specific article title from the Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes. So this has already been discussed this morning, this your limitation here or your criterion would exclude all the facts or alleged facts described in the Count 5, 6, and 7 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And deciding to base yourself on this distinction, you would automatically leave them aside.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You're not going to investigate them.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And two reasons predominantly for that rationale: Firstly, the registers, as far as I'm aware, didn't contain victim -- no, my apologies. The indictment itself doesn't contain specific names of victims, which makes it very difficult for us to cross-reference. And secondly, I don't have any knowledge of how they reached a classification of a crime at the time that these reports were formulated or at the time the registry was logged, so therefore a theft or a burglary may well have been a reported looting, but in many respects it would have been impossible for me to determine that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But this is still within the category of crimes against property.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And there you have the problem: Can I recognise something as being looting in terms of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: That was the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Was it also difficult, you said -- "We'll refrain from doing so at the moment; we have no time. "

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And it would -- the reality of it is that it would require extremely time-consuming and complex analytical work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes. It would be an investigation rather different from the one you conducted. I agree with you there. Well, I still have some other questions on your methods. You limited yourself to crimes against a person, that is clear, with a number of consequences. But when speaking about crimes against persons, I have the impression that your main tool was to work with names of individual victims, either in the indictment or in the case registers.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Then you tried to ascertain whether there would be a match.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: If there would have been a match, that would show that a case that is relevant to the indictment has arrived at the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: That's the idea, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But then the question arises: What's the significance of the fact that you have not found a match? And that is something that I would like to discuss with you. I must also say - but you have recognised this already this morning - that as far as ill-treatment or inhumane treatment of prisoners, you have only a very few names in the indictment. Most of them, presumably, were not known.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: At the time. And if you have no names of prisoners in the indictment and if you have no names of prisoners in the registers, then you have a problem; no? Your method doesn't work.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have a significant problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's suppose that there is a name in an indictment and not in the register, or let us suppose the opposite thing. First, if a victim's identity is not mentioned in the indictment, then that's the end of the search. You, even if his name or her name would be present in an indictment -- in a register, you would be unable to make a match or to do something similar. You need two names; otherwise, you cannot match.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Need ...? I'm not sure if I understand the question. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure myself. I'll try to make it -- let me try again. My point is the following: If there were names of victims in the registers where victims of events that have been described as real in the indictment --

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: If their names were not mentioned in the indictment itself, then the possibility would exist that there are cases in the prosecutor's office related to events in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: That is what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if the name was not mentioned in the indictment, you had a name, say Mr. X, in the register and you couldn't find the same name in the indictment, that would not exclude the possibility that the prosecutor may have heard him as a witness.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes, that possibility exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: We have had a number of witnesses who claimed to be a victim of ill-treatment, inhumane treatment, and whose names were not mentioned in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So that is also a restriction of -- a limitation to your investigation; yes?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: The other possibility is that -- and I am just checking with you where we are in this field -- the other possibility is that you have names of persons in the indictment but names that were not known at the time the case was investigated, but names that became apparent later; for instance, as a result of an investigation by your OTP.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, not entirely, because I've seen in -- particularly in respect of the alleged crime as Dusina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen a record - and I think the record was a list of persons names and they were the victims from Dusina where they were subjected to some form of paraffin testing, and this -- which occurred at the Zenica hospital or the Zenica morgue. And my understanding is that this list was compiled within a matter of a few days or weeks of the alleged event on the 26th of January, 1993. So for the case of -- specifically of Dusina, I would say that, you know, if they had a list of the victim names within that short a time frame, then there should have been something in the register which reflected that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I understand your reasoning, and this relates, of course, to murder or manslaughter --

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: -- cases in which there is a dead body.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: If there is a dead body, normally the dead body is identified.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: There may be unidentified dead bodies, but if the body is identified, you may be able to match.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. And there certainly were situations where the victim was clearly shown as being unidentified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yeah. But as far as victims of inhumane treatment are concerned, for instance, or persons who claimed to have been victims of that or remained in a prison or in another building. These names may not have been known at the time of a complaint or investigation.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends, I suppose, on who's making the complaint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's the victim themselves, then clearly there is no excuse for a name not to be registered or -- unless, of course, they choose to do so anonymously. I can't think of any logical explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, your assumption is that these cases only originate from complaints by individual persons and that you otherwise would not have a case.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- yeah, that is an assumption on -- to some proportion of complaints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: That may correspond to reality to some degree, but there may also be instances in which someone decides to investigate a certain situation.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So we note a fact that you repeatedly said in your report this morning and yesterday, there was no match as a result of this method of crossing names. But then what does it say? What could you conclude from it?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could only conclude that certain matters weren't referred through the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Given the uncertainties that we have discussed, I wonder whether you could really conclude that.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly for the cases of murder, I think that's the only logical conclusion that I can draw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes. But not for the other cases.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. And I'm not -- I hope I haven't misled the Court and given the impression that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that I'm asserting that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: No. You just state a fact without attaching any consequences or any interferences from it at all.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to establish.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I mean, if there was a failure to report something through to the district military prosecutor or if somebody made a determination immediately upon looking at a particular case and it didn't get referred through to the district military prosecutor, I can't make any comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So the basic problem is there here: Even if you do not find the correspondence, except, as you say, perhaps for murder and manslaughter, this doesn't say at all, or this doesn't say with certainty that there have not been cases reported.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that. I would agree with that wholeheartedly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: That's the main point that we have been discussing, I think.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I would agree with that wholeheartedly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Now, I come to my last series of questions to you. It is obvious from the beginning of your testimony yesterday and tomorrow and in answering my questions that you had to face two enormous difficulties. On the one hand, there was this enormous volume of cases, number of cases and registers, and less so case files; on the other hand, you were sent for three days.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You mentioned this as two different problems, but I would say this is the same problem.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Either you have sufficient time for a large volume of cases or you haven't. So it all boils down, then, to a problem of time.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. But unfortunately the time element still doesn't resolve those files that were missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Absolutely sure, that is. And you're absolutely correct that even if you had ten times more days at your disposal, you could not solve all these difficulties you encountered. But nevertheless, you made a number of important choices in relation to the time you had available. For instance, the choice to limit yourself to crimes against a person is such a choice.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And the choice to limit yourself to registers rather than consulting the files themselves is also such a choice.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, in many respects, is a choice that we had to make, because if the files weren't there, then the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- next option was the registers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course but if the files are not there, I understand that no matter how much time you would have, you would not be able to advance.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Another aspect might be that if you had had more time, you had probably more discussions on the question where are the missing files and where can we find them.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we would have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes. And because you had three days at your disposal, there was not the remotest possibility that you could ever do such a thing.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would say that the failure to ask that question is mine and it's mine alone. I accept responsibility for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: If somebody would have said to you, "Oh, yes, we know. They are in Sarajevo," in such-and-so street, you would have still another problem; yes?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we would have. We would have had another problem, but that could be addressed in some form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You also said at the beginning of our conversation that you did not foresee what would be awaiting you, so you came in a predicament, so to speak. If you had known before, you would have planned this investigation in a different manner; or wouldn't you have?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have certainly perhaps either tried to spend some extra time there or take some extra resources with me to try and complete the job in more detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So you would need a larger team and more time, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: To do the work properly, within parenthesis.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Properly is my qualification, do it more thoroughly, then.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. Could you give me an estimate of what you would really need to do the work in a very thorough and methodical manner and not having to confront all these limitations that you were pressed or to apply them?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we wanted to cover all the crimes against -- or property-type crimes, anything that could be looting or plundering, I think we would have probably needed another three or four days. If we had had access to every single case file and had tried to review every single case file, then it would have taken us a considerably longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, this sounds optimistic, I must say. Well, I think I have put my questions. Thank you very much for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Swart asked you some very complete questions. I would just like to ask you for some clarifications, in view of the answers that you have already provided us with. In a case of this kind in which there are victims who are known or unknown, there are violations of various kinds, crimes of various kinds, when you were involved in the investigation what were the guidelines that you were given to investigate? What sort of guidelines, what sort of instructions were you given in order to search for the truth in relation to these various crimes? This is something that occurred over five years ago, but do you remember what you were told to do, which procedure you were told to follow?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I'm a little confused. Are you talking about the entire investigation or are you talking about this particular mission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm talking about investigations in general.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, the first and foremost criteria is to establish the truth. I mean, that's the whole -- the ultimate objective of any interview. But then beyond that, if we have a series of crimes that we are looking at, then we want to get ultimately as much corroborative evidence in respect of those crimes that's available, and we are clearly told that the best means of establishing that truth and that evidence is through interviewing witnesses, searching for documents, and just, you know, normal investigative procedures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there are a number of witnesses, some of whom have testified before the Trial Chamber and some were certainly in a position to recount what happened to them. On the basis of the names of the witnesses that you disposed of, did you tell yourself that it was necessary to check in the military police's registers or in the civilian police's registers whether there were any investigations in which the names of these witnesses might appear? Was this done? If you had the names of the victims who were witnesses, did you have a look at the registers of the military police or at the registers of the civilian police, the MUP? Did you check to see whether there were any investigations conducted?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the field itself. Throughout the history of the OTP, obviously volumes of information has come in, and if such information came in about a potential witness and if thorough checks are done beforehand, then those type of things -- before you interview the person -- then those type of details should become obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have read the indictment, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In the indictment, there are the names of some individuals who were killed.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of these names, a low-ranking investigator would have to go to check these names in the registers of the military police or the civilian police to see whether there were investigations that had been conducted when these events occurred; isn't this what one should do? Was this done?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, that wasn't done, sir. No. Certainly it would have been a valuable exercise, in hindsight, to have looked at -- if it was even humanly possible, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you are aware, why wasn't this done? Why wasn't it done?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't give you any explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You went to check the registers in the court, but the registers need to be provided with documents by investigatory officials. In a court, there are two sources of information, either victims who send a letter to the military or civilian prosecutor saying that my house was burned and such-and-such a thing occurred; or the prosecutor is contacted by the investigators, by the military or civilian police and he initiates a procedure and refers the matter to the prosecutor. What is your opinion of this?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that those are two quite legitimate sources of how a complaint could commence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Because you know as a policeman that a prosecutor receives information either from victims or from policemen, from investigators, and before he goes to examine the prosecutor's -- before one goes to examine the prosecutor's registers, wouldn't it be best to check to see whether the military or civilian police had forwarded reports to the prosecutor? You're telling us that this is something that wasn't done.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Your Honour, the information that I was provided with prior to conducting this exercise was that all such referrals should have gone through the district military prosecutor. So therefore, that is the simplest point at which to, I understand, to check that these procedures have been in place. Otherwise, one would have to look at a multitude of different agencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you spent the two days there, you said you were at the site. At that time -- did you meet the prosecutor at that time? Did you see him and did you speak to the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In both courts, I spoke to the prosecutor upon my arrival, but not subsequent to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When you spoke to the prosecutor on these two occasions, you must have told the prosecutor why you were there, because if he saw someone coming from The Hague, he probably wanted to know what you were doing there. So you must have told him what you were doing there.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are nodding. When you explained what you were doing there, what was his reaction? What did he say? Did he say, "There are no problems. I'll provide you with all the documents so that you can examine them"? Or did he say that "You will perhaps find certain references but it's necessary for us to have been provided with complaints or information from investigators"? What did he tell you when you told him what you were dealing with?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought I'd made it clear yesterday that in advance of this particular mission, when preparation for it [sic], the prosecutors had been contacted before we went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Say it again, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, in preparation of going down to conduct this mission, the prosecutors had been contacted in advance and they had been asked to provide us with all the case files that had been referred through the district military prosecution service for 1993 and the early part of 1994. So when we arrived, he was expecting us and the material was available for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So just a minute. I'm reading the transcript now. You said that he was asked to provide you with all the files, with all the case files, when you arrived there, were you faced with a pile of files or did you just have registers with numbers on them? When you arrived there, what did you see? Did you see all these case files or did you see a number of registers? Because if there were case files, there must have been volumes of them.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were escorted eventually to a room that was made available for our purposes, and the case files were there, physically there, in the room. And you're quite right; there was volumes of case files, some bound neatly and others in loose piles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood you correctly, you were there and you said that there was an assistant who was also present. But if I have understood you correctly, this was someone under the prosecutor, someone who assisted the prosecutor. It's not someone who went there with you. Because since you have no knowledge of B/C/S, seeing case files in B/C/S would not be useful, so it was necessary for someone to have an understanding of the B/C/S. The person who had a look at the case files -- was that person the prosecutor's assistant or is it someone who accompanied you when you went there?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who interpreted the content of the case files or the material recorded in the register was an interpreter that we took with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this person was someone whom you took there with you. It wasn't an employee of the prosecutor. The person who read the documents was someone that went there with you from The Hague; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went there with us. We met them at the Sarajevo field office. They -- both interpreters are local interpreters who are employed by the Sarajevo field office of the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not talking about the interpreter. I'm talking about the person who was by your side in this room, the person who had a look at the case files in that room, who had a look at case file number 1. The person who had a look at the case files, who examined the case files. Who was this person? It can't have been you, as you don't know B/C/S. Who was the person who examined the case files?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of our -- one of either of two interpreters that we took with us. They read the case files and we recorded the notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But the interpreter is not a police officer or a judge or a prosecutor or a lawyer. So the person who had a look at the case files apparently didn't have any particular knowledge of criminal law or of international humanitarian law, so this way of proceeding seems to be somewhat amateurish. Why didn't you take a professional with you, someone who upon examining the case files would immediately know whether it concerned aggravated theft, simple theft, murder? Why didn't you take a professional with you? It's our impression that you asked an interpreter to tell you what the case files contained. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely it. We asked the interpreters to review, read and tell us what the contents of each case consisted of, and we made the determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But to read the legal documents takes a lot of time. It's very complicated. And if you had volumes of material in a room, how is it that you had enough time to work in a serious manner? In your opinion, this way of proceeding was a serious way to approach the problem or not?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, in my opinion, it was the only practical way of approaching it, and it is the same manner that we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not asking whether this was the only possible way. In terms of technical efficiency, was that a good way to proceed? Were there no other more efficient ways to proceed in order to eventually be able to answer the judge's questions, the prosecutor's questions, the defence's questions? Was there no other way than to place your trust in an interpreter to translate for you very complicated legal documents? So was -- an interpreter was not capable of assessing the contents of the file. Could you not approach that whole exercise in a more scientific way?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think the outcome would -- I don't think the outcome would have differed. I mean, a request for an investigation was prepared by a -- well, one of the -- either the military police or the military security organs. So it wasn't -- I don't believe it would be a scientifically difficult document to interpret. And then if an indictment was issued as a consequence, again, I don't believe that it requires a scientific background to interpret that. We certainly weren't asking the interpreter to make a scientific assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. It is half past 12.00, and we will resume in about half an hour. We will give the floor to the Defence counsel for re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the Judges' questions, I am looking at the Defence counsel. Mr. Bourgon, do you have any more questions? You have three-quarters of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is a Prosecution witness, so I would like to Prosecution to go first if they have any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just one. Further examination by Ms. Henry-Benjamin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hackshaw, for clarification sake, could you please tell us from whom you receive your instructions.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received my instructions in relation to this specific mission from both Daryl Mundis and Tecla Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But my question refers to the general basis. As acting team leader of team 9, and even as an investigator, from whom do you normally receive instructions?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: From either a member of the trial team or the deputy chief of investigations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you could take instructions from an investigator below you? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would certainly not be afraid to take instruction from an investigator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, no. It's not what you'd be afraid. What is the norm? Who -- let's say a mission is supposed to be instituted. Normally who institutes instructions with respect to missions with investigations, generally?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: The deputy chief of investigations through the chief of investigations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is his name, the chief investigator's name, that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's Mr. Patrick Lopez-Terres, and the deputy chief of investigation is Mr. Bob Reid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now on to Mr. Bourgon, if there are any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. With your permission, I would like the witness to be shown the three documents that he was shown previously. I will base my questions on those three documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we have these documents, please. What are the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to begin with the document bearing the -- bearing number "6." I am going to be referring to documents from 6 to 12. In order to facilitate the procedure for the Chamber, I would like to say that these documents refer to Dusina, Susanj, Totic, and the documents that refer to the investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Further cross-examination by Mr. Bourgon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hackshaw, I have a few quick questions for you, and my first one relates to something further to your response to the Presiding Judge concerning Dusina. You mentioned concerning Dusina that the names of the people involved were known early because you did see some kind of a document about some paraffin test. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I'm talking specifically about the victims' names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then because there was the names were known early, you concluded that there should have been a document referred to the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in response to my question earlier on, you said that you did not find any documents about Dusina and that you were in fact surprised about this issue.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when I showed you the document number 6, you did not find this document in the district military prosecutor's archives; is that correct? That's the document about Dusina, which is number 6.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me move on to document number 7, and that is Susanj. Can you confirm that Susanj was indeed an investigative issue, as the leader of team number 9?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the document which you see, document number 7, which is a document from the district military court in Zenica, that you did not find this document during your mission in June of 2004?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I move quickly to document number 9, and I don't want to repeat, because this was covered in the examination-in-chief, but just to say it once again that Totic is an investigative issue in this case.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: He certainly is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that you did not find this specific document during your mission in 2004.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me move on to document number 10, please. Document number 10 is a document from the Military Police Battalion. Do you have this document, a document dated the 20th of March, 1994?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we already confirmed based on -- at paragraph A that from the 14th of September, 1992 until 1 March of 1994 there were 377 criminal reports filed.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in response to a question, you did say that the number of files you saw yourself in Zenica was much higher.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which -- we can conclude, I suggest to you, that it means that in addition to the 3rd Corps Military Police Battalion, other units in the 3rd Corps also submitted complaints.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you never saw these 377 complaints.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we look at the next page -- no, sorry, don't look. We'll just say -- I'll keep it short. So you never saw these documents. Now, would I be right in saying that you did not possess this information until it was actually filed by the Defence as an exhibit, DH155, second document in a series of documents? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I do not think that he should be asked to answer that question. He is not a part of this trial, Mr. President, and I reiterate that this is not the witness -- aside from the fact that this did not arise out of the Judges' questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the Judges' questions, your questions have to arise from the Judges' questions, as Mrs. Benjamin has rightly said. Your question does not arise from any of the Judges' questions. I have a question of a general nature for you, Witness. There was an investigation. A procedure was underway. There was a team of investigators which always existed, team number 9. During the procedure, did you continue to follow the developments in the proceedings? Were you as a team of investigators able to follow the developments either officially or unofficially? In your capacity as an investigator, would you not be curious as to find out what the result of your investigation was? Are you abreast of what is going on in the process that you were involved with? So this is a very general question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And -- in general terms, yes; we were involved in ongoing -- all ongoing aspects to have case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To follow up on the question that was put to you: For example, during a trial there are documents that arrive, and the investigator did not see them. Would that not be a problem for you? Would you not find this a problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it -- that could be seen as a problem. There are certain persons who perform certain tasks who obviously have a -- and for example, in relation to documents, one of the criminal analysts on the team would be responsible for processing such documents, bringing them to the attention of the trial team for their more learned assessment. So although in general terms you could say yes, most people had a reasonable knowledge of all aspects. Detailed knowledge was reserved for certain persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Proceed, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to inform the Chamber that my -- that as a matter of fact it would be very important to know how come that an investigation is carried out, how it should be organised, what instructions an investigator receives. I would like to put those questions to the witness and hear from the witness how the instructions influenced the investigation. If you will allow me, I would like to ask him that as the team of investigators [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you may put that question. Anything that may help us to arrive at the truth is more than welcome. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] Item number 11 is a work entitled "On the work of the Travnik military prosecutor's office," and it is a document dated 10 January 1994. It is a document which bears the exhibit number DH119, and it is a document which was obtained by the Defence from the district public prosecutor's office in Travnik. Do you have this document, Mr. Hackshaw?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just checking now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He has the document. The witness has the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have the document now, Mr. Hackshaw?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I have 119. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is the right document. I would like to refer you to -- on this document to page 3, simply to confirm that on this page 3, paragraph 2 there is a mention that 823 criminal reports concerning 1.044 persons were received by the military district prosecutor of Travnik. Is this what you see on this document? That's page 3, paragraph 2, with the number 2.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we turn to the next page on paragraph 5. The paragraph bears the title "Breakdown of persons charged." And we see in this paragraph, if you can confirm that, 627 members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were charged during this period. Is this what you can see from this document?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what I can see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to know if this information was ever made known to you in your capacity as team leader for this investigation; if and when this information was ever made available to you.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recollect, this information wasn't something that I was familiar with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that if you were not familiar with this information, that you as the leader of team number 9 are not able to say what the 823 criminal complaints were about?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My -- the only way I would know what those individual complaints were about would be by performing the exercise that I tried to perform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I move quickly to the next document, which is document number 12. And document number 12 is a document which bears the evidence number DH274. It is a document dated 12th of December, 1993, and it was a document which the Defence obtained from the Zenica district military court. Do you have this document, Mr. Hackshaw?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I am not sure if we are following the normal path. I got the impression that this session was in respect to the Judges' questions, the issues that arose out of the Judges' questions. It seems to me that my friend is having cross-examination a second time around. He had this list before. He had the opportunity to do just this, and he failed, and it seems to me he wants another bite of the cherry, and I don't think it's very fair, unless the Prosecution is going to be given the opportunity to reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution is going to be given the opportunity to reply. The questions that you are putting to the witness, can you please clarify what they arise from.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've already explained, I'm going to use the 13 documents and the scope is to find out why he carried out the mission, what instructions he had received, and what information did he have before arriving in Bosnia. And I wanted to find out what was the information pertinent to his mission in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you may ask the questions about the last document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] And on the first page, and that is on the fourth paragraph, I believe. Yes, a paragraph which begins with "During." Now, this is something that we saw yesterday. That's just to establish the basis for my question. And yesterday you confirmed that during that year the Zenica district military court received 432 criminal cases involving 869 individuals. So that was confirmed yesterday. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was something that was presented to me, was it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, then I would agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to know if this information was made available to you in any way, and if so, when was it made available and in what form.

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That information wasn't made available to me. I didn't have any idea -- any preconceived idea about the quantity of information that would be available to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would I be right in saying, Mr. Hackshaw, that you are not able to say what exactly the number of complaints, the 432 criminal complaints filed, what they were about?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You would be correct in saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions. I just wanted to introduce documents. I want to tender these documents once we've finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team, any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we please go into private session before I start putting my questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar, can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session. Further examination by Ms. Henry-Benjamin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hackshaw, on a daily basis how often do you watch the trials in the ICTY, and in specifically the Hadzihasanovic/Kubura trial?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very rarely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you presented at any time with an update as to documents that are being marked for identification or tendered into evidence in this trial?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as you're aware -- the team 9 is composed of many part parties, but as far as you're aware, who heads the party that deals with the matter Hadzihasanovic and Kubura?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Daryl Mundis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before Daryl Mundis, who had conduct of this trial?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ekkehard Withopf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I say that the acting team leader and the deputy chief of prosecution has no conduct of this trial in any way?

utterances.speaker: PETER HACKSHAW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we do not conduct this trial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll hand document DK6 back to the registrar. This concludes your examination, Witness. As you know, sometimes investigators have to testify. This is the case in a number of countries, and it's quite normal for the chief of investigations to testify before judges. It is our understanding that this is your first time. This is the first time you have testified. You have answered all the questions put to you and the questions put to you by the Prosecution, by Defence counsel, and by the Judges, who would like to thank you for having contributed to assisting the Judges in understanding the situation, and we wish you all the best in team number 9. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thanks very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as the documents are concerned -- Mr. Bourgon, I can see that you're already on your feet. I haven't even had the time to turn towards you. What is it that you would like to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. With regard to the two documents that I would like to tender into evidence following the testimony of Mr. Hackshaw. On the list of documents we have provided, we have document number 1, which is a letter dated the 4th of June, 2004. The title is "Cases referred to district military courts relating to crimes set forth in the Third Amended Indictment." The witness had the opportunity, Mr. President, of discussing the letter, and he was familiar with the contents of the letter. As a result, we would like the letter to be admitted into evidence. And my second request concerns document number 9, Mr. President, which is a document dated the 15th of April, 1993. And the title of the document is "Record on investigation." This document comes from the district military court in Zenica and deals with the events surrounding Mr. Totic's kidnapping. The witness also stated that the kidnapping of Mr. Totic -- in fact, he spoke about everything that surrounded this event. The witness said that his attention was drawn to this issue. This is an official document that comes from the court's register, and we would like this document to be admitted into evidence. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the documents that Mr. Hadzihasanovic's Defence counsel has produced, we have two numbers. One relates to a letter dated the 4th of June, and the other document is dated the 15th of April, 1993. Ms. Benjamin, are there any objections to these two documents which were shown to the witness and the witness said that these documents were some that he had dealt with as an investigator? Are there any objections you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we should raise any objections if in fact the witness had dealt with the documents, but I think the witness in some instances said that he was now seeing them for the first time and on the face of it, it looks okay. That to me would not have been the proper foundation that we would want from a witness in order to tender same into evidence. But if the Trial Chamber is satisfied with the foundation that was laid, the Prosecution has no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have two final exhibit numbers for these two documents, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document dated the 4th of June, 2004 gets the exhibit number DH339. The document dated the 15th of April, 1993 gets the exhibit number DH340, and its English translation gets the exhibit number DH340/E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have one last document which was presented by Mr. Kubura's Defence counsel. This document refers to another document that was admitted. There is a correlation between these two documents. Ms. Benjamin, any objections to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And definitely this one we're going to object to because this witness has nothing to do with this document. He knew not of the document. And he couldn't assist the Court in any way, and I can't see how my friend could want a document like this to be tendered through a witness like this. This is not the appropriate witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will give this document a final exhibit number but it will be under seal, as it should be considered as a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will have the number DK14, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DK14, under seal. Thank you. Any other issues to raise, Mr. Bourgon? I was going to turn to the issue of the other documents that we mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would just like to say that tomorrow I will be making submissions to clarify the situation about the files that were shown by one of the Judges to the witness. I would like to clarify the situation, to show where the documents came from. I'll do that tomorrow, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yesterday the Prosecution -- but we will go into private session first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: I will see everyone tomorrow at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 30th day of June, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.,
